claim: The Regulation applies to specified providers, deployers, importers, distributors, product manufacturers, authorised representatives and affected persons connected with the Union.
qualifiers: Providers may be established in the Union or a third country when placing AI systems, putting them into service, or placing general-purpose AI models on the Union market.
Deployers are covered when established or located in the Union.
Third-country providers and deployers are covered when AI-system outputs are used in the Union.
Affected persons are covered when located in the Union.

claim: For Article 6(1) high-risk AI systems related to products governed by Annex I Section B legislation, only the provisions enumerated in Article 2(2) apply.
qualifiers: The enumerated provisions are Article 6(1), Articles 102 to 109 and Article 112.
Article 57 applies only insofar as AI Act high-risk requirements have been integrated into the relevant harmonisation legislation.

claim: The Regulation excludes matters outside Union-law competence and does not affect Member State competences in national security.
qualifiers: The identity or type of entity performing national-security tasks does not alter this boundary.

claim: AI systems are excluded insofar as they are placed on the market, put into service or used exclusively for military, defence or national-security purposes.
qualifiers: The exclusion applies with or without modifications and regardless of the type of actor.
Outputs used in the Union are also excluded when the system is not marketed or put into service there and the outputs are used exclusively for those purposes.

claim: AI systems, AI models and their outputs are excluded when specifically developed and put into service solely for scientific research and development.
qualifiers: Both specific development and sole scientific research-and-development purpose constrain the exclusion.

claim: Pre-market or pre-service research, testing and development activities concerning AI systems or models are excluded, but real-world testing is not.
qualifiers: Excluded activities must still comply with applicable Union law.

claim: Union personal-data, privacy and communications-confidentiality law continues to apply to personal data processed in connection with AI Act rights and obligations.
qualifiers: The AI Act does not affect the listed data-protection instruments, subject to the stated Article 10(5) and Article 59 qualifications.

claim: An AI system is an automated system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy that may adapt after deployment and infers from inputs how to generate outputs capable of influencing physical or virtual environments.
qualifiers: Objectives may be explicit or implicit.
Outputs include predictions, content, recommendations or decisions.

claim: AI systems released under free and open-source licences are generally excluded from the Regulation.
qualifiers: The exclusion does not apply when such a system is placed on the market or put into service as high-risk, within Article 5, or within Article 50.

claim: The Regulation leaves other Union consumer-protection and product-safety rules unaffected.
Union and Member State rules or collective agreements may provide workers with more favourable protection concerning employer use of AI systems.
Obligations on deployers do not apply to natural persons using AI systems in a strictly personal, non-professional activity.
A deployer is an actor using an AI system under its own authority, except for personal non-professional use.
qualifiers: Actors may include natural or legal persons, public authorities, agencies or other bodies.

claim: Operator is the collective term for a provider, product manufacturer, deployer, authorised representative, importer or distributor.
A provider is an actor that develops or has developed an AI system or general-purpose AI model and markets it, or puts the AI system into service, under its own name or trademark.
qualifiers: Actors may include natural or legal persons, public authorities, agencies or other bodies.
Provision may be for payment or free of charge.

claim: Risk combines the probability of harm with its severity.
Putting into service means supplying an AI system for first use directly to a deployer or for own use in the Union according to its intended purpose.
Reasonably foreseeable misuse is use outside the intended purpose that can result from reasonably foreseeable human behaviour or interaction with other systems, including AI systems.
A safety component performs a safety function for a product or AI system, or creates danger to persons’ or property health and safety if it fails or malfunctions.

Intended purpose is the provider-intended use of an AI system, including its specific context and conditions of use as described in instructions, advertising or sales material, statements and technical documentation.
Conformity assessment is the procedure for demonstrating compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements for a high-risk AI system.
A substantial modification is an unanticipated post-market or post-service change that harms compliance with Chapter III Section 2 requirements or changes the intended purpose assessed.
qualifiers: The change was not foreseen or planned in the provider’s initial conformity assessment.

claim: Training data are data used to train an AI system by adjusting its trainable parameters.
Validation data evaluate the trained AI system and tune its non-trainable parameters and learning process, including to avoid underfitting or overfitting.
Biometric data are personal data resulting from specific technical processing of a natural person’s physical, physiological or behavioural characteristics.
qualifiers: Examples given are facial images and fingerprint data.

claim: Biometric verification is an automated one-to-one identity check, including authentication, against biometric data previously supplied by the person.
Biometric identification automatically recognises human characteristics to establish a natural person’s identity by comparing their biometric data with stored biometric data of persons.
Special categories of personal data are the categories referred to in the GDPR, Law Enforcement Directive and Union-institution data-protection provisions cited by Article 3(37).
Real-time remote biometric identification performs acquisition, comparison and identification without significant delay.
qualifiers: Slight delay remains real-time when needed to prevent circumvention.

claim: An emotion-recognition system recognises or infers a natural person’s emotions or intentions from biometric data.
A biometric-categorisation system assigns natural persons to specific categories on the basis of biometric data.
qualifiers: A function merely ancillary to another commercial service and strictly necessary for objective technical reasons is excluded from this definition.

claim: A remote biometric-identification system identifies natural persons without their active involvement, generally at a distance, by comparing their biometric data with a database.
Post-remote biometric identification is remote biometric identification other than real-time remote biometric identification.

Placing on the market, putting into service or using AI that employs subliminal, deliberately manipulative or deceptive techniques is prohibited when the specified behavioural and harm conditions are met.
qualifiers: The technique must have the objective or effect of materially distorting a person’s or group’s behaviour by appreciably impairing informed decision-making.
It must cause a decision that would not otherwise have been taken.
It must cause or be reasonably likely to cause significant harm to that person, another person or a group.

temporal_effect.basis: The pre-existing Article 5 rules are within Chapters I and II, applicable from 2 February 2025; the 2 December 2026 deferral is limited to newly inserted points (ba), (bb), paragraph 1a and paragraph 1b.

claim: Placing on the market, putting into service or using AI that exploits vulnerabilities linked to age, disability, or a specific social or economic situation is prohibited when the specified behavioural and harm conditions are met.
qualifiers: The objective or effect must be materially to distort the behaviour of the person or a member of the group.
The distortion must cause or be reasonably likely to cause significant harm to that person or a third party.

temporal_effect.basis: The pre-existing Article 5 rules are within Chapters I and II, applicable from 2 February 2025; the 2 December 2026 deferral is limited to newly inserted points (ba), (bb), paragraph 1a and paragraph 1b.

claim: AI systems that create or expand facial-recognition databases through untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV are prohibited.
qualifiers: The prohibition covers placing on the market, putting into service for that specific purpose, or using such systems.

temporal_effect.basis: The pre-existing Article 5 rules are within Chapters I and II, applicable from 2 February 2025; the 2 December 2026 deferral is limited to newly inserted points (ba), (bb), paragraph 1a and paragraph 1b.

claim: Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes is prohibited except where strictly necessary for an enumerated objective.
qualifiers: Objectives shown on this page are targeted searches for specified victims or missing persons and prevention of specified serious threats to life, physical safety or terrorist attack.
The further enumerated criminal-investigation objective continues on Page 175.

temporal_effect.basis: The pre-existing Article 5 rules are within Chapters I and II, applicable from 2 February 2025; the 2 December 2026 deferral is limited to newly inserted points (ba), (bb), paragraph 1a and paragraph 1b.

claim: AI inference of a natural person’s emotions in workplaces or educational institutions is prohibited.
qualifiers: Medical or safety reasons are excepted.
The prohibition covers placing on the market, putting into service for that specific purpose, or use.

temporal_effect.basis: The pre-existing Article 5 rules are within Chapters I and II, applicable from 2 February 2025; the 2 December 2026 deferral is limited to newly inserted points (ba), (bb), paragraph 1a and paragraph 1b.

claim: Biometric categorisation that individually categorises natural persons to deduce or infer specified sensitive attributes is prohibited.
qualifiers: Specified attributes include race, political opinions, trade-union affiliation, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life and sexual orientation.
Lawfully acquired biometric datasets may still be labelled or filtered on biometric data, and biometric data may be categorised in law enforcement.
The prohibition covers placing on the market, putting into service for that specific purpose, or use.

temporal_effect.basis: The pre-existing Article 5 rules are within Chapters I and II, applicable from 2 February 2025; the 2 December 2026 deferral is limited to newly inserted points (ba), (bb), paragraph 1a and paragraph 1b.

claim: The Article 5(1)(h) rule does not affect GDPR Article 9 for biometric processing outside law enforcement.
A permitted law-enforcement use of real-time remote biometric identification may be deployed only to confirm the identity of the specifically targeted person.
qualifiers: The use must consider the seriousness, probability and scale of harm if not used and the consequences for the rights and freedoms of all affected persons.

temporal_effect.basis: The pre-existing Article 5 rules are within Chapters I and II, applicable from 2 February 2025; the 2 December 2026 deferral is limited to newly inserted points (ba), (bb), paragraph 1a and paragraph 1b.

claim: The real-time remote biometric-identification exception includes locating or identifying a criminal suspect for investigation, prosecution or execution of a criminal penalty under defined offence and penalty thresholds.
qualifiers: The offence must be listed in Annex II.
In the Member State concerned it must carry a maximum custodial sentence or detention order of at least four years.

claim: A permitted law-enforcement use of real-time remote biometric identification must comply with necessary and proportionate safeguards and conditions under authorising national law.
qualifiers: Safeguards include temporal, geographical and personal limitations.
The authority must complete an Article 27 fundamental-rights impact assessment and register the system under Article 49.
In a duly justified emergency, use may start before registration if registration follows without undue delay.

temporal_effect.basis: The pre-existing Article 5 rules are within Chapters I and II, applicable from 2 February 2025; the 2 December 2026 deferral is limited to newly inserted points (ba), (bb), paragraph 1a and paragraph 1b.

claim: Each such law-enforcement use requires prior authorisation from a judicial authority or a binding independent administrative authority in the Member State of use.
qualifiers: The request must be reasoned and follow national rules.
In a duly justified emergency, use may start before authorisation if authorisation is requested without undue delay and no later than 24 hours.
If refused, use must stop immediately and all data, results and outputs from the use must be discarded and deleted immediately.

temporal_effect.basis: The pre-existing Article 5 rules are within Chapters I and II, applicable from 2 February 2025; the 2 December 2026 deferral is limited to newly inserted points (ba), (bb), paragraph 1a and paragraph 1b.

claim: The competent authorising authority may approve real-time remote biometric identification only when objective evidence or clear indications show it is necessary and proportionate for an enumerated purpose.
qualifiers: Use must be strictly limited in time and geographical and personal scope.
No decision producing adverse legal effects may be based solely on the system output.

temporal_effect.basis: The pre-existing Article 5 rules are within Chapters I and II, applicable from 2 February 2025; the 2 December 2026 deferral is limited to newly inserted points (ba), (bb), paragraph 1a and paragraph 1b.

claim: Each law-enforcement use of real-time remote biometric identification in a public space must be notified to the relevant market-surveillance and national data-protection authorities.
qualifiers: Notification follows national rules and contains at least the Article 5(6) information.
Notification must exclude sensitive operational data.

temporal_effect.basis: The pre-existing Article 5 rules are within Chapters I and II, applicable from 2 February 2025; the 2 December 2026 deferral is limited to newly inserted points (ba), (bb), paragraph 1a and paragraph 1b.

claim: Notified national market-surveillance and data-protection authorities must report annually to the Commission on such real-time remote biometric-identification use.
qualifiers: The Commission supplies a reporting template covering authorisation decisions and outcomes.

temporal_effect.basis: The pre-existing Article 5 rules are within Chapters I and II, applicable from 2 February 2025; the 2 December 2026 deferral is limited to newly inserted points (ba), (bb), paragraph 1a and paragraph 1b.

claim: The Article 6(1) product route requires the AI system to be intended as a safety component of an Annex I product or itself to be such a product.
qualifiers: This is the first of two cumulative conditions; the second continues on Page 180.

claim: The Commission must publish annual reports on law-enforcement use of real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces.
qualifiers: Reports use aggregated Member State data and exclude sensitive operational information.

temporal_effect.basis: The pre-existing Article 5 rules are within Chapters I and II, applicable from 2 February 2025; the 2 December 2026 deferral is limited to newly inserted points (ba), (bb), paragraph 1a and paragraph 1b.

claim: Article 5 does not displace prohibitions arising under other Union-law provisions.

An Annex III AI system is not high-risk when it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing decision outcomes, and a listed condition is met.
qualifiers: Listed conditions are a narrow procedural task, improvement of a previously completed human activity, pattern or deviation detection without replacing or influencing prior human assessment absent proper human review, or a preparatory task for an Annex III assessment.
The profiling override continues on Page 181.

temporal_effect.basis: Chapter III Sections 1, 2 and 3 apply from 2 December 2027 for Article 6(2) and Annex III systems, except Article 6(5).
temporal_effect.binding_use_condition: Any obligation or high-risk classification claim must retain this future application date.

claim: The Commission may amend the Article 6(3) derogation conditions by delegated act when concrete and reliable evidence shows Annex III systems do not pose significant risk to health, safety or fundamental rights.
qualifiers: The power is exercised under Article 97.

claim: A provider treating an Annex III AI system as not high-risk must document that assessment before market placement or putting into service.
qualifiers: The provider must register the system under Article 49(2).
The provider must supply the assessment documentation when requested by a competent national authority.

temporal_effect.basis: Chapter III Sections 1, 2 and 3 apply from 2 December 2027 for Article 6(2) and Annex III systems, except Article 6(5).
temporal_effect.binding_use_condition: Any obligation or high-risk classification claim must retain this future application date.

claim: An Annex III AI system that profiles natural persons is always high-risk despite the Article 6(3) derogation.
Annex I completes Section A with in-vitro diagnostic medical devices and begins Section B with other harmonisation legislation.
qualifiers: The Section B entries on this page cover civil-aviation security, two- or three-wheel vehicles and quadricycles, agricultural and forestry vehicles, marine equipment and rail-system interoperability.

temporal_effect.basis: Chapter III Sections 1, 2 and 3 apply from 2 August 2028 for Article 6(1) and Annex I systems, except Article 6(5).
temporal_effect.binding_use_condition: Any high-risk classification claim must retain this future application date.

claim: Annex I Section B includes harmonisation legislation for motor-vehicle type approval, market surveillance and general vehicle safety.
qualifiers: The listed instruments are Regulation (EU) 2018/858 and Regulation (EU) 2019/2144.

temporal_effect.basis: Chapter III Sections 1, 2 and 3 apply from 2 August 2028 for Article 6(1) and Annex I systems, except Article 6(5).
temporal_effect.binding_use_condition: Any high-risk classification claim must retain this future application date.

claim: Annex I Section B includes specified civil-aviation legislation insofar as it concerns design, production and marketing of specified unmanned aircraft and related components.
qualifiers: The entry covers the aircraft in Article 2(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 and their engines, propellers, parts and remote-control equipment.

temporal_effect.basis: Chapter III Sections 1, 2 and 3 apply from 2 August 2028 for Article 6(1) and Annex I systems, except Article 6(5).
temporal_effect.binding_use_condition: Any high-risk classification claim must retain this future application date.

claim: Annex II begins the offence list used by the Article 5(1)(h)(iii) real-time remote biometric-identification exception.
qualifiers: The page includes terrorism, trafficking in human beings, child sexual exploitation and abuse material, drug trafficking, arms trafficking, intentional homicide and serious injury, organ or tissue trafficking, nuclear or radioactive-material trafficking, kidnapping or hostage-taking, International Criminal Court crimes, and aircraft or ship hijacking.

temporal_effect.basis: The Annex II list supports the pre-existing Article 5(1)(h) exception; the amending act's Article 5 changes and Annex amendments do not replace Annex II, while the pre-existing Article 5 provisions are already applicable.

claim: Annex II completes the offence list used by the Article 5(1)(h)(iii) exception.
qualifiers: The page adds rape, environmental crime, organised or armed robbery, sabotage, and participation in a criminal organisation involved in one or more listed offences.

temporal_effect.basis: The Annex II list supports the pre-existing Article 5(1)(h) exception; the amending act's Article 5 changes and Annex amendments do not replace Annex II, while the pre-existing Article 5 provisions are already applicable.

claim: Annex III lists specified biometric AI as high-risk where its use is permitted by applicable Union or national law.
qualifiers: Listed uses are remote biometric identification, sensitive or protected-attribute biometric categorisation, and emotion recognition.
Biometric verification solely confirming that a specific person is who they claim to be is excluded from the remote-identification item.

temporal_effect.basis: Chapter III Sections 1, 2 and 3 apply from 2 December 2027 for Article 6(2) and Annex III systems, except Article 6(5).
temporal_effect.binding_use_condition: Any high-risk classification claim must retain this future application date.

claim: Annex III lists AI safety components used to manage or operate specified critical infrastructure as high-risk.
qualifiers: Covered infrastructure is critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, and supply of water, gas, heating or electricity.

temporal_effect.basis: Chapter III Sections 1, 2 and 3 apply from 2 December 2027 for Article 6(2) and Annex III systems, except Article 6(5).
temporal_effect.binding_use_condition: Any high-risk classification claim must retain this future application date.

claim: Annex III lists specified educational and vocational-training AI uses as high-risk.
qualifiers: Uses cover access, admission or assignment; learning-outcome assessment including learning guidance; evaluation of an appropriate educational level; and monitoring or detection of prohibited exam behaviour.
The educational scope covers institutions at all levels.

temporal_effect.basis: Chapter III Sections 1, 2 and 3 apply from 2 December 2027 for Article 6(2) and Annex III systems, except Article 6(5).
temporal_effect.binding_use_condition: Any high-risk classification claim must retain this future application date.

claim: Annex III lists AI intended for recruitment or selection of natural persons as high-risk.
qualifiers: Examples include targeted job advertisements, application analysis and filtering, and candidate evaluation.

temporal_effect.basis: Chapter III Sections 1, 2 and 3 apply from 2 December 2027 for Article 6(2) and Annex III systems, except Article 6(5).
temporal_effect.binding_use_condition: Any high-risk classification claim must retain this future application date.

claim: Annex III lists specified AI uses in employment and worker management as high-risk.
qualifiers: Uses include decisions affecting work relationships, promotion or termination; task allocation based on behaviour, personality traits or personal characteristics; and performance or behaviour monitoring and evaluation.

temporal_effect.basis: Chapter III Sections 1, 2 and 3 apply from 2 December 2027 for Article 6(2) and Annex III systems, except Article 6(5).
temporal_effect.binding_use_condition: Any high-risk classification claim must retain this future application date.

claim: Annex III lists specified AI uses affecting access to essential private services, public services and social benefits as high-risk.
qualifiers: Uses cover public-authority eligibility and benefit decisions, personal creditworthiness or credit scores except financial-fraud detection, life and health insurance risk assessment or pricing, and emergency-call evaluation or prioritisation, emergency dispatch, and emergency-healthcare triage.

temporal_effect.basis: Chapter III Sections 1, 2 and 3 apply from 2 December 2027 for Article 6(2) and Annex III systems, except Article 6(5).
temporal_effect.binding_use_condition: Any high-risk classification claim must retain this future application date.

claim: Annex III lists specified law-enforcement AI uses as high-risk where authorised by applicable Union or national law.
qualifiers: Uses shown are victim-risk assessment, polygraphs or similar tools, evidence-reliability assessment, and offending or reoffending risk assessment that is not based solely on profiling, as well as assessment of personality, characteristics or criminal history.
Covered users include law-enforcement authorities and Union institutions, bodies or agencies, including actors acting for or supporting them.

temporal_effect.basis: Chapter III Sections 1, 2 and 3 apply from 2 December 2027 for Article 6(2) and Annex III systems, except Article 6(5).
temporal_effect.binding_use_condition: Any high-risk classification claim must retain this future application date.

claim: Annex III includes law-enforcement profiling used in criminal-offence detection, investigation, prosecution or execution of criminal penalties among high-risk uses.
qualifiers: The provision references profiling under Article 3(4) of Directive (EU) 2016/680.

temporal_effect.basis: Chapter III Sections 1, 2 and 3 apply from 2 December 2027 for Article 6(2) and Annex III systems, except Article 6(5).
temporal_effect.binding_use_condition: Any high-risk classification claim must retain this future application date.

claim: Annex III lists specified AI uses for migration, asylum and border-control management as high-risk where authorised by applicable Union or national law.
qualifiers: Uses shown are polygraphs or similar tools, individual security, irregular-migration or health risk assessment, and assistance with asylum, visa or residence-permit applications and related complaints, including evidence-reliability assessment.

temporal_effect.basis: Chapter III Sections 1, 2 and 3 apply from 2 December 2027 for Article 6(2) and Annex III systems, except Article 6(5).
temporal_effect.binding_use_condition: Any high-risk classification claim must retain this future application date.

claim: The Commission guidelines describe a four-tier AI Act risk framing and state that Article 5 screening addresses practices presented as unacceptable risk.
qualifiers: Commission interpretation; the guidelines expressly state that they are non-binding.
uncertainties: Risk categories and legal effects require confirmation against the reviewed AI Act text.

claim: Article 5 screening is described as a case-specific assessment; examples in the guidelines are indicative rather than determinative.
qualifiers: Assessment depends on the facts and conditions of the individual use case.
uncertainties: The guideline does not supply an exhaustive decision procedure.

claim: The guidelines distinguish placing an AI system on the Union market, putting it into service for first use or own use, and using it after those events when scoping an Article 5 assessment.
qualifiers: The real-time remote biometric identification category is described as applying specifically to use.
uncertainties: Definitions cited from the AI Act require confirmation against the binding source.

claim: For Article 5 screening, the guidelines focus on provider and deployer responsibility and describe Union establishment, Union market activity, or use of system output in the Union as relevant connecting factors.
qualifiers: Role and territorial scope depend on the facts and the AI Act definitions.
uncertainties: Actor qualification must be confirmed against reviewed binding provisions.

claim: The guidelines interpret use broadly across the lifecycle and across integration into services, processes, infrastructure, or larger systems, including misuse that may amount to a screened practice.
qualifiers: This is Commission interpretation and is non-binding.
uncertainties: The breadth of misuse coverage needs binding-source and case-specific review.

claim: A deployer is described as the organisation or person that controls the decision and manner of professional system use; staff or contractors acting under an organisation’s procedures and control are generally treated as acting for that deployer.
qualifiers: Personal non-professional activity is treated separately.
uncertainties: Responsibility allocation remains fact-specific and requires binding-source review.

claim: One operator may simultaneously hold provider and deployer roles, so an Article 5 gate should record each role and the control exercised over design, supply, and actual use.
qualifiers: Role accumulation can arise for in-house development and use.
uncertainties: Downstream duties for each role are outside this extraction and require binding evidence.

claim: The guidelines describe the military, defence, and national-security exclusion as purpose-based and limited to systems used exclusively for those purposes.
qualifiers: Entity identity alone does not establish the exclusion.
uncertainties: The meaning of national security and exclusive purpose requires legal review against binding authority.

claim: A dual-use system offered for both excluded and non-excluded purposes is described as remaining within AI Act scope for the non-excluded route, while use exclusively for national-security, defence, or military purposes may remain excluded.
qualifiers: Purpose and actual use must be separated in the assessment record.
uncertainties: Application to mixed or changing purposes is case-specific.

claim: The guidelines describe a separate exclusion for specified third-country or international-organisation judicial or law-enforcement cooperation where adequate fundamental-rights safeguards are present.
qualifiers: The cooperation framework and safeguards are both material conditions.
uncertainties: Competent-authority assessment and binding-source confirmation are required.

claim: Pre-market research, testing, or development activity and systems developed and put into service solely for scientific research are described as scope exclusions, subject to distinct limits.
qualifiers: Real-world testing and later market placement or putting into service are treated separately.
uncertainties: The two research exclusions have different conditions that require binding-source confirmation.

claim: The personal non-professional exclusion is described as affecting deployer obligations for qualifying natural-person use rather than removing every other actor or legal framework from consideration.
qualifiers: Professional, economic, representative, or criminal activity is described as outside this narrow personal-use framing.
uncertainties: Other Union and national laws may still apply.

claim: The guidelines describe the free and open-source exclusion as unavailable when the system is placed on the market or put into service as high-risk, within an Article 5 category, or within the specified transparency route.
qualifiers: Licence status alone does not conclude the scope analysis.
uncertainties: Exact conditions require review against the binding AI Act text.

claim: A system associated with an Annex III use may require both Article 5 screening and high-risk classification because a specific deployment can meet a screened-practice condition even when the broader use category is high-risk.
qualifiers: Article 5 and Article 6 gates are related but yield distinct outcomes.
uncertainties: Exceptions and classification routes must be confirmed from binding evidence.

claim: The guidelines state that an Article 6(3) non-high-risk outcome does not remove the system from Article 5 screening.
qualifiers: The Article 5 gate remains independently applicable.
uncertainties: The legal effect must be confirmed against reviewed binding provisions.

claim: The guidelines apply Article 5 screening to systems with a specific intended purpose and to general-purpose systems used directly or integrated into another system.
qualifiers: Responsibility is described as depending on role and control in the value chain.
uncertainties: Measures for general-purpose systems are expressed as Commission expectations, not binding conclusions in this source.

claim: The guidelines recommend proportionate safeguards, use restrictions, instructions, human oversight, and responsive action when a provider becomes aware of a screened misuse.
qualifiers: Measures depend on the provider’s control, available information, feasibility, and the system context.
uncertainties: Monitoring must be assessed under applicable Union law and cannot be inferred as universally required from this non-binding source.

claim: Passing the Article 5 gate is described as insufficient to establish compliance with other applicable Union law, including data protection, equality, employment, consumer, and fundamental-rights rules.
qualifiers: Parallel legal regimes may restrict a use that is not captured by Article 5.
uncertainties: The applicable parallel regime depends on actors, data, purpose, sector, and jurisdiction.

claim: For certain law-enforcement biometric uses, the guidelines describe the AI Act and data-protection rules as operating together and state that the AI Act does not itself supply a personal-data processing legal basis.
qualifiers: The described interaction is limited to specified biometric and law-enforcement contexts.
uncertainties: This specialised legal interaction requires authoritative legal review before use as a rule.

claim: An Article 5 exception is described as incapable of justifying non-compliance with another applicable Union-law obligation.
qualifiers: The Article 5 and parallel-law assessments must be recorded separately.
uncertainties: Exact legal consequences require confirmation from binding sources.

claim: The Commission guidelines treat AI-system determination as the threshold step for AI Act scope and call for a system-specific assessment rather than mechanical use of an exhaustive list.
qualifiers: The guidelines expressly state that they are non-binding.
uncertainties: The controlling definition and legal effects require confirmation against the reviewed AI Act text.

claim: The guidelines use a lifecycle view in which definition elements may appear during building or use and need not remain continuously observable in both phases.
qualifiers: Assessment should consider pre-deployment and post-deployment characteristics.
uncertainties: The evidential threshold for each element is not fully specified on this page.

claim: The guidelines decompose the AI-system definition into seven elements: machine basis, varying autonomy, possible post-deployment adaptiveness, explicit or implicit objectives, inference from inputs, specified output categories, and possible influence on physical or virtual environments.
qualifiers: The decomposition is interpretive guidance for applying Article 3(1).
uncertainties: Each element must be audited against binding text before publication as a rule.

claim: The guidelines distinguish an internal explicit or implicit system objective from the provider-defined intended purpose and deployment context.
qualifiers: Internal objectives can arise from encoded goals, training data, or interaction with an environment.
uncertainties: Intended-purpose evidence may also depend on documentation and workflow integration described beyond this page.

claim: The level of autonomy is described as relevant to risk mitigation and human-oversight design, especially in high-risk contexts.
qualifiers: The appropriate oversight depends on intended purpose and the use context.
uncertainties: This source does not define a universal autonomy threshold.

claim: Post-deployment adaptiveness is described as optional: a system can meet the AI-system definition without self-learning or behavioural change after deployment.
qualifiers: Autonomy and adaptiveness are treated as distinct concepts.
uncertainties: Binding confirmation is required because this is non-binding interpretation.

claim: The capability to infer how to generate outputs is treated as the key distinction from software that only executes rules fully specified by natural persons.
qualifiers: The guidance links inference to both model or algorithm derivation and output generation.
uncertainties: Borderline deterministic and rules-based systems require case-specific technical evidence and binding-source review.

claim: The guidelines interpret inference across the building and use phases rather than limiting it to producing an output from a given input at runtime.
qualifiers: The underlying techniques used to build the system are relevant to this interpretation.
uncertainties: The boundary between covered inference and ordinary software remains fact-sensitive.

claim: The output element is described through four broad categories: predictions, content, recommendations, and decisions.
qualifiers: The categories differ in function and degree of human involvement.
uncertainties: A system output may require contextual classification where categories overlap.

claim: The guidelines present very basic statistical baselines and static mean estimators as examples outside the AI-system definition despite their possible use of elementary learning methods.
qualifiers: The examples concern basic benchmark performance rather than a general exemption for all statistical systems.
uncertainties: This boundary is interpretive, potentially fact-sensitive, and must not be treated as a binding safe harbour.

claim: The guidelines distinguish recommendations that remain subject to human evaluation from decisions that directly produce an outcome without human intervention.
qualifiers: Automatically applying a recommendation may change its functional classification.
uncertainties: Actual workflow and human influence must be evidenced rather than inferred from product labels.

claim: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 is an amending act for Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 concerning implementation of harmonised AI rules.
qualifiers: The act is dated 8 July 2026 and the Official Journal page identifies publication on 24 July 2026.
uncertainties: Page 1 is marked REVIEW_REQUIRED and needs independent local fidelity review.

claim: For Article 6(1) high-risk systems, the act explains that AI Act requirements may be limited where Annex I Section A legislation supplies equivalent protection, provided the AI Act protection level is preserved.
qualifiers: This recital explains the purpose of the operative Article 2(13) amendment on Page 16.

claim: The amendment targets the safety-component concept to systems capable of adversely affecting the health and safety of persons or property, because that concept determines part of the Article 6(1) high-risk classification gate.
qualifiers: This is recital-level explanation; the operative definition appears on Page 16 and Article 6 clarifications on Page 18.

claim: The act states that Article 5 is amended to address AI systems generating non-consensual intimate material and child sexual abuse material.
qualifiers: This recital gives the legislative rationale; the operative prohibitions appear on Page 18.

claim: The recitals distinguish provider and deployer conditions for the new prohibited-content practices and limit the deployer prohibition to purposeful generation or manipulation of the specified material.
qualifiers: Provider conditions turn on intended purpose or a reasonably foreseeable and reproducible outcome without adequate safeguards.
uncertainties: The operative wording on Page 18 controls the legal test.

claim: The child-sexual-abuse-material prohibition preserves cases covered by a national-law 'without right' defence, including legitimate authority activity and legitimate compliance evaluation described in the recital.
qualifiers: The operative cross-reference is to Directive 2011/93/EU and national law.
uncertainties: Applicability of the national-law defence requires jurisdiction-specific legal review.

claim: The act explains that the application dates for Chapter III Sections 1 to 3 are moved to 2 December 2027 for Article 6(2)/Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for Article 6(1)/Annex I systems.
qualifiers: This is recital-level explanation; the operative Article 113 amendment appears on Page 35.

claim: The act explains that machinery legislation is moved from Annex I Section A to Section B so that the limited Article 2(2) AI Act regime applies to those machines while sector legislation incorporates specified protections.
qualifiers: The operative Annex I amendment appears on Page 36.

claim: Amended Article 2(7) confirms that Union data-protection, privacy and communications-confidentiality law applies to personal data processed in connection with AI Act rights and obligations.
qualifiers: The provision is without prejudice to Articles 4a and 59 and states that the AI Act does not affect the listed data-protection instruments.

claim: For Article 6(1) high-risk AI systems related to products under Annex I Section B, amended Article 2(2) limits AI Act application to Article 6(1), Article 60a and Articles 102 to 112.
qualifiers: Articles 57, 58 and 59 apply only where high-risk requirements have been integrated into the relevant harmonisation legislation.

claim: New Article 2(13) permits specific requirements or obligations in Articles 9 to 15 and 17 to 25 for Article 6(1) systems to be limited only where Annex I Section A legislation provides equivalent or higher protection and the overall AI Act protection level is not reduced.
qualifiers: The concrete systems, requirements, conditions and extent of any limitation depend on delegated acts.

claim: The Commission must adopt delegated acts by 2 August 2027 specifying the Article 2(13) high-risk systems and the requirements, conditions and scope of permitted limitations.
qualifiers: The delegation concerns Article 6(1) systems and the limits described in Article 2(13).

claim: Amended Article 3(14) defines a safety component by its safety function or by whether its failure or malfunction endangers persons' or property health and safety; a safety function has the intended purpose of preventing or mitigating such risks.
qualifiers: This definition feeds the Article 6(1) high-risk classification gate.

claim: For deployers, Article 5(1a) applies the new prohibited-content rules only when the system is used for the purpose of generating or manipulating the specified material or performance.
Article 6(1c) states that a product does not satisfy Article 6(1)(b) when third-party conformity assessment is required solely for risks unrelated to health and safety.
qualifiers: The provision gives spectrum distribution and non-health electromagnetic interference as examples.

claim: For providers, Article 5(1a) applies the new prohibitions where generation or manipulation is the system's intended purpose, or is a reasonably foreseeable and reproducible outcome without significant technical modification and adequate preventive and corrective safeguards are absent.
qualifiers: The test considers design, training, architecture, capabilities, user-facing functions and reasonably foreseeable misuse.

claim: Article 6(1b) classifies an AI system as a safety component when its failure or malfunction would endanger health and safety, notwithstanding Article 6(1a).

New Article 6(1a) excludes from the safety-component classification systems used solely for non-safety aspects of user assistance, performance optimisation, service efficiency, automation, convenience or quality control.
qualifiers: The exclusion is limited by Article 6(1b).

claim: Article 5(1b) excludes from the intimate-material manipulation concept changes that neither increase exposure of depicted intimate parts nor alter the nature of depicted sexually explicit activity.

For Annex I Section A products, classification as high-risk under Article 6(1) does not itself remove a conformity-assessment option allowed by the relevant harmonisation legislation or require third-party assessment solely because a high-risk safety component is present.
qualifiers: Any standards-based option remains subject to applying standards or common specifications covering all Chapter III Section 2 requirements.

claim: Providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended for use by public authorities must take the necessary compliance steps by 2 August 2030.

For pre-existing high-risk systems outside Article 111(1), the amended transition rule generally applies the AI Act after the relevant Chapter III date only where the system design is significantly changed from that date.
qualifiers: High-risk systems intended for use by public authorities are subject to a separate compliance deadline of 2 August 2030.

claim: Chapter III Sections 1, 2 and 3 apply from 2 December 2027 to systems classified as high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III, except Article 6(5).
Chapter III Sections 1, 2 and 3 apply from 2 August 2028 to systems classified as high-risk under Article 6(1) and Annex I, except Article 6(5).
AI Act Articles 102 to 110 apply from 27 July 2026 under the amended Article 113 schedule.
The new Article 5(1)(ba) and (bb) prohibitions and their Article 5(1a) and (1b) conditions apply from 2 December 2026.
